description_en: The things to listen for are the heavy octaves of the opening Largo and the sad Moderato melody that follows. Pianists differ enormously in how they convey the weight of the first note and the sorrow of the melody.
After the turbulent first theme, the mood changes completely and a dreamy melody in E♭ major appears. It is regarded as the most beautiful passage in Chopin’s Ballade No. 1.
Explosive chords arrive under the marking “Il più forte possibile” (as loudly as possible); after a brief pause to catch its breath, the music races ahead in a frenzy.
Rachmaninoff Piano Concerto, first movement.
Rachmaninoff Piano Concerto, second movement.
Rachmaninoff Piano Concerto, third movement.
Pianists choose between the ossia and the original version of the first-movement cadenza, which makes it a good passage for comparison.
A comparison of the highlights of the second movement.
From the climax of the second movement to the finale of the third.
The introduction to the second movement.

Prelude No. 7 of the 24 is a sixteen-bar, mazurka-like miniature in A major. Short phrases with the same rhythm follow one another eight times, and in the middle of the second half one widely spread chord rings out. Performances differ in **how much they hold back the phrases before that chord**.

Variation 1 is a 3/4 variation in which two voices chase each other. The score asks for both the first and second halves to be repeated. **Gould skips both repeats**, which makes his the shortest version of this variation, at 1:10.

The first piece of Grieg’s Lyric Pieces, Arietta. A high melody sings while a calm figure flows beneath it. After the melody rises once to a big moment, it returns to the first theme and closes quietly. The three performances differ most in **how loudly the first note is played**.

A short Étude in G♭ major, lasting about a minute. The right hand moves without pause between two successive notes and short, detached octaves; the music swells in the middle, then the first motif returns and the piece closes on a motif that climbs upward. All three performances last about a minute, and they differ in **whether the build to the middle happens in one go or after stepping back once**.

A piece in B minor depicting a game of tag. Fast sixteenth notes run as if chasing and being chased, and in the opening section a gesture repeats in which the first note is struck hard and immediately drops to soft (sfp). It lasts only about 30 seconds, so performances differ in **how fast it runs and how loudly it ends**.

The very beginning of the work. A high D♯ rings like a bell, and the right hand leaps between that bell and the melody below. The score says to play softly but keep the theme clear (ben marcato). The three performances differ most in **how closely they keep to this “softly”**.
The last 20 seconds or so, where octaves and chords come crashing down. Performers differ in whether they play at full force from the start or build up toward the end.

The opening of Tchaikovsky’s Concerto No. 1. The horns call out briefly in B♭ minor, then move to D♭ major, where the strings sing the big melody and the piano supports it with wide chords. This melody never returns after the introduction. All three performances are loudest in the first 10 seconds, and they differ in **how far they bring the volume down afterward**.

Coming straight from the previous movement without a pause, the finale bursts out in a C major tutti. The trombones, piccolo and contrabassoon join here for the first time, and the first theme, which climbs up the tonic chord, rings out thickly. Each performance holds **the loud playing for a different length of time**.

The opening of the Fifth Symphony. The four-note motif is hammered out twice, followed by a long pause, and then the strings pass the motif back and forth softly, building it up. All three performances share this shape, and they differ in **how deeply the quiet passage sinks**.

A short waltz also known as the “Minute Waltz.” It begins with a figure in which the right hand circles round and round the same spot; a melody sings leisurely in the middle, and the circling figure returns for a brief close. Some performances put **the loudest moment** early, others after the circling figure has returned.

An étude that begins with a slow E major song, surges fast in the middle, and then returns to the first song. The right hand alone sings the melody on top while also playing the accompaniment beneath it. In the middle both hands move quickly in double notes and rise to the loudest point. The three performances differ most in **how softly the first song is kept**.

Over a slow triple meter, the left hand alternates between a low bass note and a chord while the right hand lays a plain melody on top. The accompaniment begins first and the melody then enters; the same course is followed almost exactly twice, with only the ending different. Performances differ in **how loudly the piece ends**.

The complete Moments Musicaux No. 3 by Schubert. Over a short, detached left-hand accompaniment, the right hand lays an F minor dance melody; it is a miniature of about two minutes. When it was first published it was given the title “Air russe” (a Russian-style song). Performances place **the loudest moment** differently.

The complete “Für Elise.” The A minor theme that begins with the right hand alternating E and D♯ returns three times, and between the returns come a bright F major section and a dark section in which a low A repeats without pause. All three performances are about the same length, and they differ in **where the loudest point falls**.

A piano piece in which Ravel borrowed the slow tread of the pavane, an old court dance. The first theme returns three times, with another melody intervening twice, and at the end the first theme comes back in thick chords. Performances divide on **how loudly they close that final return**.

An intermezzo played between scenes of the opera Thaïs. Over the harp’s gentle arpeggios, a solo violin sings a long melody; the melody rises and intensifies in the middle, then returns to the opening melody and ends quietly on a high note. The three performances differ most in **how deeply the music sinks after the big moment in the middle**.

A nocturne that Chopin wrote at twenty and that was published after his death. It sings with slow, expressive feeling (Lento con gran espressione), and in the middle it draws on a melody from his own Piano Concerto No. 2. At the end, quick ornamental figures pour from the right hand. Performances differ in **when they first play loudly**.

An overture strung together from melodies in the operetta Die Fledermaus. It opens with a short tutti, followed by a slow song and a fast dance, and the waltz that is the work’s best-known number flows out among them. In all three performances the loudest sound comes at the same place, and they differ in **how loudly the first tutti is opened**.

A fast polka in which the bass drum’s thunder and the cymbals’ lightning break in without pause. It begins with a short tutti, a lively theme runs, passes through the central trio, then returns to the first theme and ends in a rush. In all three performances the last chord is loudest, and **how long the loud playing is sustained** differs.

A piece that paints water leaping from a fountain on the piano. The right hand keeps up a finely splintering figure without pause, while short melodies rise and sink among it. In all three performances the loudest point comes about a quarter of the way from the end. The performances differ in **how deeply the quiet passages sink**.

The whole first movement, in which a dotted-rhythm melody rises over a triplet accompaniment. Beethoven wrote that it should be played from beginning to end very softly and delicately, with the dampers raised (senza sordino). In all three performances the loudest point comes about a third of the way in, and the **tempo** differs so much that one performance is more than a minute shorter than the other two.

Throughout the slow second movement, the same song-like melody appears three times. The theme, which begins in the middle register, is soon repeated an octave higher and returns after each of two middle sections that lean toward the minor. From the second middle section on, the accompaniment changes to fine triplets. In all three performances the loudest point comes a little past the middle, and they differ in **how far they bring it down afterward**.

The complete “Clair de lune.” It starts with soft chords, grows in the middle as left-hand arpeggios spread beneath, and at the end **the first theme returns over the arpeggios**. All three performances follow the same course, and they differ in length and in how loudly the first note is played.

It begins with a bell-like motif of three descending notes, sounded very loudly. Soft chords follow, then in the middle the Agitato section speeds up and rushes ahead, and the opening motif returns in thick chords written across four staves. The three performances differ most in **how long they sustain the returning bells at full volume**.

A piece in F major built on a melody that begins with a soft upward leap and keeps returning. The same phrase starts again and again, unchanged or at a different pitch, and near the end it pauses at length on the highest note before fading to soft. Performances differ in **where the singing is loudest and how wide the dynamic range is**.

The whole third movement, which begins with soft arpeggios that surge upward and collide with two loud chords. A second theme in G♯ minor follows soon after, and near the end the music halts briefly on a two-bar slow passage (Adagio) before closing on a very loud chord. Two performances play loudest more than a minute before the end, and one plays **the final chord loudest**.

The whole finale of the “Pathétique.” Sections in E♭ major, A♭ major and C major interrupt the C minor rondo theme in turn, and near the end the theme glimmers in A♭ major once before closing in C minor. The same movement differs by nearly a minute between performances, **from 3:59 to 4:57**.

The whole Ballade, from the slow introduction to the fiery coda. The soft first theme in G minor and the second theme in E♭ major, which enters in a whisper, return in changed keys, and later the second theme swells twice to a very loud ff. Performances differ in **where the loudest sound is placed**.

The whole aria in which Calaf, beginning with “Nessun dorma” (“Let no one sleep”), proclaims victory at dawn. It opens quietly over a soft orchestra; the main melody soars once and settles, then rises again on the final “Vincerò” (“I shall win”), and the orchestra takes it up and closes. The three performances differ most in **how loudly the first peak is sung**.

A movement in the simplest sonata form. The right hand sings a C major theme while the left hand supports it with an Alberti bass. After a passage in which scales flow down at length, the second theme appears in G major, and in the recapitulation the first theme returns in F major. None of the three performances swings the dynamics much, and **the place where each plays loudest** differs.

The whole first movement, which opens with the strings rising in unison on a G major chord. After the vigorous call, a violin song follows, and soon the graceful second theme in D major appears. The same opening returns in the recapitulation. All three performances share the same course, and they differ in **whether the first call or the last chord is made louder**.

A piece depicting Mazeppa, tied to a horse’s back and galloping across the fields. Within chords divided between the two hands, the D minor theme rings out like hoofbeats; in the middle it sinks once as if singing, then surges again and ends in D major. Performances differ in **how deeply the quiet passages sink**.

A rhapsody in two parts, a slow lassan and a fast friska. The C♯ minor lassan opens solemnly in low octaves, and the friska begins softly and gradually speeds up into a dance. Near the end the score leaves a cadenza to the performer. Performances differ in **how they close after the climax**.

The passage where the first-movement cadenza begins. Rachmaninoff left this cadenza in two versions: the long ossia, which piles up heavy chords, and the short original, which runs lightly. **Only Lang Lang plays the ossia**, so this passage is about 50 seconds longer in his performance.

The introduction that opens the Ballade, and the first theme in G minor. The introduction draws out a melody doubled in octaves and stops on an unresolved chord; the theme starts softly and grows steadily fiercer. The five performances differ most in **how long they keep the music quiet**.

The passage where the second theme in E♭ major enters in a whisper (sotto voce). Over wide left-hand chords the right hand sings a melody in doubled voices, and soon starts the same melody once more. The four performances differ in **how quietly and how late it enters**.

The coda that ends the Ballade. The tempo becomes fiery fast (Presto con fuoco), and the right-hand chords are accented between the beats, pushing forward. The left hand alternates between low bass notes and chords, supporting those off-beats. The five performances differ in **whether they come in loudly from the start and how far they pull back before the end**.

The final movement of Haydn’s Trumpet Concerto, in which a lively rondo theme, introduced softly by the strings, keeps returning. It was written for the new keyed trumpet, which can play chromatic notes, so scalar melodies that the old trumpet found hard to produce run through it. Performances differ in **whether the loudest sound falls on the last chord or in the middle of the movement**.

A movement in which the solo horn brings out a hunting-style rondo theme in 6/8, and the theme returns again and again with other sections in between. Each time the theme comes back, the orchestra takes it up. In all three performances the theme is cycled evenly, and **the place of the loudest sound** differs.

The D major tutti opens with a rising arpeggio, and the violins run lightly through the first theme. The second theme is a comical melody in which the violins leap a wide interval, and the first theme returns in C major. In all three performances the tempo and overall shape are the same, and they differ in **how deeply the quiet passages sink**.

A trill in the woodwinds and a rising figure in the strings set up a galloping ground, over which the brass shout out a theme in 9/8. The theme returns again and again, shifting position, and each time it comes back different instruments carry it. The three performances differ most in **whether the loudest sound is placed in the middle of the piece or at the end**.

An overture painting the sea around the Hebrides, the islands off Scotland. Violas, cellos and bassoons bring out a short motif in B minor, and this motif returns throughout. After a fierce rush at the end, it closes softly. The three performances differ in **whether the loudest sound is in the middle or in the final rush**.

A fast movement in G♯ minor that drives on without rest. The four instruments dig in at very loud volume and hardly pause for breath until the end, and amid them a Jewish-style melody taken from Piano Trio No. 2 soars sharply. The three performances differ most in **how long they sustain the loud playing**.

A piece that begins with a single right-hand line and grows into two and then three interwoven lines. Very slow (Sehr langsam) and without a tonal center, short fragments of melody pass back and forth and then disappear into a quiet last note. The three performances differ most in **how softly the first single line is opened**.

A toccata movement (Precipitato) driving on without rest in 7/8. The left hand obstinately repeats the same low figure while chords hammer above it, ending in a rush to the final B♭ octave. In all three performances the loudest point comes at the end, and the **tempo** differs so that they range from 3:09 to 3:36.

The whole slow second movement of the concerto Shostakovich wrote for the birthday of his son Maxim. The strings open a soft introduction in C minor, the piano enters with a quietly singing melody, and the movement closes on a soft piano chord. In all three performances the loudest point comes right in the middle, and the **length ranges from six minutes to seven and a half**.

The D major concerto opens with a soft string introduction. After the orchestra rises once and falls back, the solo violin brings out a brief statement alone and then sings the first theme. Each performance sets **the dynamics and length of the introduction** differently.

The slow movement, the Romanze, begins with a simple B♭ major song that the piano brings out alone. As this song returns several times, the piano rushes in with fast figuration in the G minor section at the center and the scene suddenly changes. Each performance treats **the dynamics of the opening song** differently.

The “Emperor” Concerto begins with a big chord from the orchestra, answered by the piano with an improvisation-like flourish. This exchange occurs three times over three chords, E♭, A♭ and B♭, after which the orchestra brings out the first theme. The three performances differ most in **whether the loudest sound is in the first reply or at the very end**.

The opening of the G minor symphony, in which the violins bring out the first theme softly over the violas’ fine accompaniment. The theme, which keeps repeating a sigh-like two-note motif, bursts out forcefully in a tutti, and then the second theme follows, moving to B♭ major and sliding down in semitones. Performances differ in **how early and how long they play loudly**.

The last movement opens with a fanfare in which the whole orchestra hurls out a dissonance at once. Then the cellos and double basses declaim a recitative as if speaking, calling up the openings of the previous movements one by one and rejecting them. The three performances differ in **which of the two fanfares is hit harder**, and in length.

The Rite of Spring begins with a melody that a single bassoon sings alone in a very high register. Soon the English horn and clarinets layer in different melodies of their own, and as woodwinds join one by one, the sound thickens. Each performance plays **the bassoon’s first sound** at a different volume.

A piece that moves from a fast C♯ minor section to a slow D♭ major song and back to a fast section. In the outer sections four right-hand sixteenth notes play against the left hand’s triplets, and in the middle a relaxed song (Moderato cantabile) unfolds. Performances differ in **whether the loudest sound falls in the first section or in the returning section**.

Liszt’s piano transcription of one of his own songs, in which a mid-range melody sings amid arpeggio accompaniment. After a short cadenza the melody is sung again in a changed key and reaches a boiling climax, and after a second cadenza it returns to the original key. In all three performances the climax comes at the same place. What differs is **how deeply the music sinks after the climax**.

A waltz in which a desolate minor-key melody flows over an oom-pah-pah accompaniment. The whole orchestra takes up the melody that the saxophone first presents and builds it up; near the end it shrinks once and then returns big. Performances differ in **how loudly the first melody is opened**.

A set of twelve variations on the melody best known as “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star.” It darkens into the minor in Variation 8, Variation 11 sings as a slow Adagio, and Variation 12 changes to 3/4 and ends energetically. Performances place **the loudest moment** differently, and their lengths differ by more than a minute and a half.

The clarinet opens the piece by sliding up in a single sweep from a low trill. After that, the first theme flows in jazz style and the orchestra takes it up. In all three performances the loudest point is near the end, and they differ in **how low they keep the music before that**.

The final piece that closes Carnaval, a march in which the League of David (Davidsbündler) drives out the Philistines. Though a march, it walks in three-beat time, and an old dance tune mocking stale taste, the “Grossvatertanz,” breaks in. After material from the first piece returns, the music speeds up and rushes to the end. **Whether loud playing is used from the start or held back until the end** is what separates the three performances.

The whole Impromptu in G♭ major, in which a long melody sings over ceaselessly flowing arpeggios. The first melody continues, darkens into the minor, rises up once to a big moment, and then returns to the opening melody and closes. Performances differ in **how widely the dynamics rise and fall**.

The opening of Liszt’s symphonic poem: after the strings’ pizzicato, a short three-note motif rises like a question. As this motif repeats, shifting position, the orchestra swells little by little, until at the end the whole ensemble rings out loudly. In all three performances the loudest point comes at the end, and they differ in **whether the music builds once early on and then settles back**.

The opening section of the piece depicting an American walking the streets of Paris. Strings and woodwinds step out the light walking theme, and even taxi horns break in as the street starts to bustle. In all three performances the shape is the same: the loudest playing comes about a minute in, then drops sharply. They differ in **how early the volume is raised**.

The final two minutes or so, which close the piece after the battle, with bells and cannon. The chant melody first sung by the low strings returns in full orchestra, and as the music speeds up the brass sing the Russian imperial anthem while the cannons sound. Each performance chooses differently between **opening at maximum from the start and building toward the end**.

The introduction in which, after an orchestral hit and a descending piano chord, the oboe brings out the first theme in A minor. The piano soon takes over the same theme and sings it, and gradually builds strength together with the orchestra. Performances differ in **whether the first descending chord or the big passage later on is played loudest**.

The passage where the slow movement (Larghetto) of Chopin’s Concerto No. 1 begins. Muted strings open the way softly, and then the piano enters singing the E major theme. All three performances begin softly and grow, and they differ in **whether the music settles back after one big song**.

The concerto begins when the orchestra throws out a short, resolute theme and the piano answers forcefully in octaves. After this big exchange the music sinks deep for a while and rises again at the end. **How deep and how long the sinking passage is held** is different in every performance.

The passage that gave the symphony its nickname, “Surprise.” After the soft theme is played twice, at the end of the second statement the whole orchestra suddenly strikes loudly. **How softly the lead-up to that one blow is laid down** differs from performance to performance.

The opening, in which cellos and double basses bring out the B minor introduction very softly. As the violins spread out finely, oboe and clarinet sing the first theme together, and after one big surge the cellos present the second theme in G major. The three performances share this shape, and they differ in **how softly the opening is kept**.

As soon as the movement opens, the winds repeat the same chord rapidly and the violins bring out the A major first theme with big leaps (Allegro vivace). The theme soon spreads to the whole orchestra and rings out loudly, and later all three performances drop to soft once. The performances differ in **how deeply they let this soft passage sink**.

The passage where, just after the orchestra’s soft accompaniment has barely begun, the solo violin sings the E minor first theme in a high register. With no long orchestral introduction, the soloist steps in right away, lifts the theme high, and then the whole orchestra takes up the same theme loudly. In all three performances the loudest point comes around the middle, and the **tempo and the loudness of the first note** differ.

The opening of the Adagio, where the clarinet sings the D major theme alone and the orchestra takes up the same melody and repeats it. The same song is heard once with the solo instrument and once with the full ensemble. The three performances differ most in **whether the loudest singing comes early or late**.

The first movement (Allegretto) begins with the cello alone bringing out a four-note motif. The orchestra soon enters and exchanges this short motif with the cello, and the sound grows in size as the passage goes on. Performances differ in **when the music climbs to its loud passages**.

The finale opens with a four-note motif: C–D–F–E (do–re–fa–mi). The violins bring out the motif softly, a vigorous tutti follows, and soon the strings start a fugato in which they stack the same motif one by one. The three performances share this course, and they differ in **how softly the first motif is brought out**.

The symphony’s nickname, “The Clock,” comes from this passage. Bassoons and pizzicato strings tick evenly like a pendulum, and above them the first violins lightly lay a melody in G major. In all three performances there is one big rise about two-thirds of the way in. The same passage takes anywhere **from 1:18 to 1:41**, so the pace of the steps differs greatly.

The final section of the “Farewell” Symphony, in which the players finish one by one and leave. It is said to have been written to tell the prince that the orchestra, long confined to the summer palace, wanted to go home. Instruments drop out one after another until only two violins remain at the end. All three performances grow quieter, and they differ in **how much they thin out toward the end**.

The hymn-like introduction (Andante non troppo) that opens the first movement of the Serenade for Strings. The string ensemble lowers a C major melody heavily in thick chords, then gradually settles into the fast section. All three performances cover the same passage, and the **tempo ranges from 1:38 to 2:26**.

The opening of the movement that Beethoven titled “Awakening of cheerful feelings upon arrival in the country.” The short theme that the strings bring out softly soon halts on a fermata, and then the theme’s short motif repeats many times and spreads through the whole orchestra. All three performances follow the same course, and they differ in **whether the loudest sound is placed at the early peak or at the end**.

After a woodwind chord in A minor, the low strings begin by softly repeating a rhythm of long–short–short–long–long. This repeated rhythm (ostinato) forms the basis of the movement, and when the theme has made one round, the higher strings take it over. In all three performances the first chord is loudest, and they differ in **how deeply the quiet passage after it sinks**.

The passage where the timpani open the concerto by beating out a Charleston rhythm. The orchestra takes up that rhythm and unfolds a jazz-style introduction, and the piano enters alone only after the orchestra has worked itself up. Performances differ in **whether they play loudly from the very start or build up step by step**.

The opening of the concerto, a slow melody (Andante) sung softly by a solo clarinet. Soon the strings speed up and move into the fast section, and the piano drives in with the busy first theme. In all three performances the loudest point comes at the end, and **how softly the clarinet introduction is played** differs.

Although this is a concerto, the solo violin has not yet appeared in these two minutes or so; the orchestra opens the stage. The timpani strikes a D softly five times, the woodwinds sing the first theme, and the violins then hit an unfamiliar D♯ in the same rhythm. The three performances differ most in **how softly the timpani opening begins**.

The violin begins by singing the spring theme over the piano’s gentle broken chords. When one round of the theme ends, the piano takes over the same theme and the violin steps back to support it. The three performances differ most in **where the music builds to its loudest point**.

The third movement opens by repeatedly striking diminished seventh chords. The chords pour down in sixteenth notes into an unbroken flow, over which the F minor theme runs. The three performances differ most in **whether the very first chord is played at full volume**.

A rondo in which a pattering theme in A minor and a vigorous march in A major alternate, ending in A major. As a movement imitating Ottoman military bands (alla turca), it has a march section in which the left-hand chords sound like drums. The three performances divide on **how far they come down when returning to the soft theme**.

The theme of the movement that takes the music of the song “Death and the Maiden” and continues with variations. The four instruments move as one in almost the same rhythm, walking like a slow chorale in G minor. The step of one long note followed by two short ones continues to the end. Performances differ in **how softly the quiet passages are kept**.

The opening of the movement that continues as variations on the melody of the song “The Trout.” While the piano rests, the violin, viola, cello and double bass present the theme plainly in D major. The three performances differ most in **how long the loud playing is sustained**.

In this third movement (Poco allegretto), Brahms put a rather relaxed song in place of a scherzo. The cello sings a C minor theme low, with the strings supporting it in a flowing accompaniment, and soon the violins take over the same song. In all three performances the loudest singing comes near the end, and they differ in **when the first loud singing occurs**.

The first two minutes or so of the “Eroica” Symphony’s second movement, where the funeral march begins. The first violins offer the C minor march theme under their breath, with the double basses’ short grace notes beneath supporting it like drums. Soon the oboe takes up the same theme. Performances differ in **when the build-up to a loud sound begins**.

The opening of Symphony No. 1 (Un poco sostenuto), where the timpani beat a C without a break while the strings climb in semitones and the woodwinds descend against them. After this weighty opening passage, the sound sinks to soft and the woodwinds step forward. Each performance differs in **whether the opening passage or the loud sound at the end is played louder**.

The variation theme that opens the slow third movement. The piano first brings out a hymn-like melody in D major, and the violin and cello enter and take up the same melody. In all three performances the loudest point is near the end, and they differ in **when they first come near full volume**.

The introduction to the first movement, which opens with the cello alone singing the first theme low, in D minor. The piano lays down a restlessly turning accompaniment, and as the violin joins, the three drive the theme loudly together. In all three performances the loudest point is right in the middle, and they differ in **how early they come close to full volume**.

The introduction to the first movement opens with a stately E♭ major first theme sounded by all five instruments at once. After the first theme the volume drops a notch, and the music moves to the second theme, in which the viola takes up a song that the cello started. In all three performances the first theme is played loudest, and they differ in **how deeply the second theme sinks**.

The opening of the finale (Adagio lamentoso), which closes the symphony with a slow lament. The strings bring out a lament theme descending in B minor; this melody is shared note by note between the first and second violins, so it is not written out whole on either line. In all three performances the loudest point is early on, and the **tempo and the depth to which the middle sinks** differ.

An introduction in which the full orchestra surges straight into the E♭ major first theme without a prelude. Though in triple time, a hemiola, in which the accents group two beats at a time across the bar lines, overlays it, so the beats seem to surge broadly. The three performances differ most in **whether they play at full volume from the first theme or hold back until later**.

The first violins open the symphony with a sighing figure, descending notes in thirds paired two by two. The woodwinds support the softly presented theme in between, and as the theme goes on it grows until the whole orchestra rings out forcefully. All three performances follow almost the same course, and they differ slightly in **when they come close to full volume**.

The chorus from Act 3 of Lohengrin that leads Elsa and Lohengrin to the bridal chamber, whose melody is commonly known as the wedding march. After a short orchestral introduction the chorus sings the first melody (Treulich geführt), softens briefly in the middle, and then the first melody returns. In all three performances the loudest point falls at the same place, and they differ in **how softly the beginning and end are kept**.

A song in which a single singer moves among four roles (narrator, father, son and the Erlking) over a triplet accompaniment that hammers like horse hooves. The son’s cry of “Father” rises higher each time, and at the end the accompaniment stops, leaving a single phrase. In all three performances the loudest point comes late in the song, and they differ in **how softly the ending is closed**.

Bartók’s “night music” begins. The xylophone strikes a single note, first quickening and then slowing, and the timpani slides the pitch upward. Then the violas bring out a melody low, and the celesta and harp add sparkling sounds. In all three performances the loudest point comes about 20 seconds before the end, and they differ in **how low the middle is kept**.

The opening of the slow movement, in which the low strings slowly build dark, low chords and a solo horn then sings at length. The woodwinds speak between the horn phrases, and as the music goes on it rises to a big sound. In all three performances the loudest point comes 20 to 30 seconds before the end, and they differ in **how early the volume is raised at the beginning**.

“Game of the Pairs” opens with a rhythm played by the snare drum alone, and the wind instruments come in one pair after another. The first pair, two bassoons, walk side by side a sixth apart, and the two oboes that follow stay close together in thirds. In all three performances the music peaks right in the middle, and they differ in **how loudly they continue after that**.

After a brief woodwind introduction, the harp unfolds a long cadenza alone, the horn brings out the D major waltz theme, and the clarinet answers. In the middle the woodwinds and low strings sing a new melody, and then the waltz returns and heads toward a brilliant close. The three performances differ most in **whether the loudest sound comes at the very end**.

Music depicting the feud between two families. Harsh dissonances announcing the Prince’s command confront hushed strings, then a heavy march theme steps out, and in the middle the sound suddenly lightens as a soft dance melody flows. Performances differ in **the length of the hushed passage between the two outcries**.

The Swan theme appears. Over the harp’s arpeggios and the strings’ tremolo the oboe brings out the theme in B minor, and the theme spreads through the whole orchestra, rises loudly, and sinks again. Each performance sets **the volume of the oboe’s first song** differently.

A dance that three puppets, brought to life by the magician’s flute, suddenly perform in the middle of the fair. The piano drives chords within the orchestra and pulls along a folk-style melody, sinks softly once in the middle, and returns with the original energy. The three performances divide on **whether the loudest sound comes early or at the end**.

The dance that the demon king Kashchei and his followers perform, under the Firebird’s spell, until they fall down exhausted. The whole orchestra opens with striking chords, and syncopated rhythms hitting the off-beats drive it on to the end. In all three performances the loudest playing comes at the end, and they differ in **how deeply they let the music sink before that**.

The famous wedding march, opened by a trumpet fanfare, familiar from weddings. Between the stately C major march sections, a much gentler middle section intrudes, and then the march returns. **The point at which the playing first reaches near-maximum volume** differs by more than three minutes between performances.

The opening of the first movement, in which the orchestra lays out the theme before the solo violin enters. Low strings and woodwinds bring out the first theme in D major softly, then the whole orchestra rises up loudly and settles again. With no soloist yet, the difference lies with the conductor and orchestra. Performances differ in **how softly the first theme is played**.

It opens with the scene from Richard Dehmel’s poem in which two people walk under the moonlight through a cold, bare wood. In D minor, very slow (Sehr langsam), it begins with a theme in which the low strings step down one step at a time, and grows gradually from a soft sound. In all three performances the loudest point comes near the end, and the same passage takes anywhere **from 2:01 to 2:34**.

The opening of the Prologue, in which the two gangs first confront each other. Over finger snaps a tritone motif rises, and this unsettling interval spreads on a jazz rhythm, building tension. In all three performances the loudest point comes near the end, and they differ in **how softly the lead-up is drawn out**.

An overture the composer made by stringing together song melodies from his own operetta. It opens with a tutti fanfare from the orchestra and runs fast, then midway the melody of the love duet flows leisurely before the music rushes to the end. The three performances differ most in **when they start playing near maximum volume**.

The overture opens with the clarinets, bassoons and horns softly singing the Pilgrims’ Chorus theme. Soon the strings overlay a sighing, undulating melody, and the Pilgrims’ theme grows louder and spreads through the full orchestra. In all three performances the loudest point comes at the end, and they differ in **how softly the first chorus is brought out**.

The aria in which the Queen of the Night urges her daughter to kill Sarastro. There are two coloratura passages in which the voice leaps in staccato up to a high F. The big picture is the same in all three performances, and they differ in **how far the dynamics sink between the coloratura passages**.

The aria in which the Duke of Mantua lightly sings that a woman’s heart changes like a feather in the wind. The orchestra first plays the melody, and as two verses are sung to the same melody in B major, the orchestra takes it up again between them. In all three performances the loudest point is the final cadence, and they differ in **how much is held back while singing**.

The march from the Act 2 scene in which the Egyptian army enters in triumph. Long trumpets on stage play a fanfare melody in A♭ major, and then other trumpets raise the same melody to B major and play it again. In all three performances the last chord is loudest, and where they differ is **how loudly the fanfare starts**.

The drinking song (Brindisi) from the Act 1 party, in which Alfredo raises his glass first and Violetta answers with the same melody. The chorus takes up the lively B♭ major melody verse after verse, and at the end the two exchange lines before everyone rushes together toward the final chord. In all three performances the last chord is loudest, and they differ in **how loudly the prelude opens**.

The opening of the Requiem’s second movement, the “Dies irae” (“Day of Wrath”), which sings of the Day of Judgment. The bass drum pounds on off-beats between the chords that the full orchestra strikes down, and while the chorus shouts, the strings sweep in fast scales. In the final passage the chorus mutters in a hushed voice. The three performances differ most in **how low they let this final passage sink**.

The fourth of the seven movements, set in the middle, sings Psalm 84 gently in E♭ major in triple time. It rises once in the middle, and near the end it rises again as the voices take up “they praise you evermore” in turn. Performances differ in **which of the two climaxes is played bigger**.

The last piece of the Requiem’s Sequence. The chorus sings over a sighing figure in the strings, and after the first eight bars that Mozart left, his pupil Süssmayr completed it. In all three performances the music is loudest at the end of the opening section, in which the chorus creeps upward by semitones. Each performance sets **the dynamics of the first sound** differently.

Symphony No. 7 begins with the strings striding out the C major first theme forcefully. The theme rises loudly once and surges again, and at the end the sound sinks deep as the music moves into a quiet section. The three performances differ most in **how many seconds it takes to reach the maximum**.

The opening of the Symphony of Psalms, which begins with the orchestra striking a short E minor chord. Since the scoring omits violins and violas, small woodwind figures fill the gaps between the chords, and then the altos begin a prayer in a narrow melody that moves between two notes. In all three performances the course is the same, and they differ in **how deeply they let the spaces between chords and the middle sink**.

The final movement opens as a march. Over the timpani’s beats the brass thrust out the D minor march theme forcefully, then the tempo gradually quickens and the whole orchestra drives the theme on. All three performances come in loudly from the first beat, and they differ in **where the loudest sound is placed**.

The passage in The Creation where light first appears in the darkness. Raphael intones the first verse of Genesis low, and the chorus continues very softly, and at “Und es ward Licht” (“And there was light”) the chorus and orchestra burst out all at once in C major. All three performances share this shape, and **the time it takes to reach the light** differs.

The fifth song of Winterreise. The piano opens with a prelude like rustling leaves; the first verse in major darkens into minor, and rises loudly at the passage where the cold wind rushes. In all three performances this wind passage is loudest, and they differ in **the tempo of the song**.

The song that opens the sixteen-song cycle Dichterliebe. The same melody is sung for two verses, and the piano prelude returns between the verses and at the end. Even after the song ends, the piano stops on an unresolved chord and hands the question on to the next song. The three performances differ most in **how softly the piano prelude opens**.

An introduction depicting the noise of the big city. The strings race on chromatically without pause, and the brass break in roughly above them. The section extends to the moment when the noise surges on for a while and then suddenly subsides. Performances differ in **when they get close to maximum volume and how long they hold it**.

The cello alone opens by rising softly, and the woodwinds place the famous Tristan chord at the end of its phrase. This question-like phrase repeats at ever higher pitches with silences between, until at last the whole orchestra rises up loudly for the first time. The same passage ranges **from 1:37 to 2:06**.

A C minor miniature lasting under a minute, heard from start to finish. A line of sixteenth notes runs almost without rest between the two hands and ends on a closing chord. None of the three performances varies the dynamics much. **The place of the loudest sound** and the length differ.
